    Wing lift curve

      How the numbers are computed, and how accurate they are
      • Wing, tailplane and fin are solved together with a vortex lattice (Weissinger's extended lifting line, a horseshoe vortex on every strip with flow tangency at three-quarter chord). So tip losses, sweep, taper and twist shape the span loading, the tail feels the wing's downwash, and the stall starts wherever a strip first reaches its section maximum. Checked against theory: an elliptic wing of aspect ratio 8 gives a lift slope of 4.88 per radian and a span efficiency of 0.998.
      • Induced drag comes from the far-wake (Trefftz-plane) wash of the same lattice, with a viscous factor (Nita–Scholz). Compressibility scales the lattice with Prandtl–Glauert below Mach 1 and Ackeret theory above it; swept wings get leading-edge vortex lift (Polhamus).
      • NACA zero-lift angle and pitching moment come from thin-airfoil theory on the actual mean line. Section CLmax is an empirical fit by thickness and camber; slats add about 0.6.
      • Skin friction is Prandtl–Schlichting on every strip, with Raymer's form factors and wetted areas. Transonic drag rise uses the Korn equation; supersonic wave drag uses Raymer's Sears–Haack estimate from the largest cross-section.
      • Propellers: efficiency rises with airspeed to a peak, and static thrust is capped by momentum theory. Jets: thrust lapses with air density, the intake loses pressure above Mach 1, and thrust fades once the ram-heated air at the engine face passes about 127 °C. Engine weight is sized from power or thrust using real engines.
      • Structure: wings fail at 1.5 times the limit load factor, and the airframe breaks up about 22 % past its never-exceed speed. Skin temperature follows the boundary-layer recovery temperature. The airspeed indicator shows calibrated airspeed.
      • Checked against real aircraft: the Trainer lands within about 15 % of a Cessna 172 on stall and top speed. The Fighter could reach about Mach 1.3 at sea level (past its 800 kt never-exceed speed, as in an F-16) and Mach 1.9 at 36,000 ft, against an F-16's Mach 2.05. Not modelled: propwash, engine torque, flaps, gusts. Treat results as good first estimates.

      Make a plane that flies

      Everything the designer asks you to set comes down to a handful of ideas: four forces, how a wing makes lift, what drag costs, and where the weight sits. Read this once and every number in the designer will make sense.

      Is your design fly-ready?

      These checks run on the design open in the designer, using the same physics you fly. Fix anything marked Fix before you fly. Check means it will fly but needs care.

        The four forces

        Every aircraft in flight is a tug-of-war between four forces. Lift from the wing holds it up against weight. Thrust from the engine pulls it forward against drag from the air. In steady, level flight they balance exactly: lift equals weight and thrust equals drag.

        In the designer, weight is the mass items on the Airframe tab plus the wings and tails. Lift comes from the Wing tab. Thrust comes from the engine on the Airframe tab. Drag comes from everything the air touches.

        How a wing makes lift

        A wing is shaped and tilted so that the air leaving its trailing edge is thrown downward. Pushing air down pushes the wing up. How much lift you get follows one equation:

        Lift = ½ × ρ × V² × S × CL

        ρ (rho)
        Air density. It falls with height: at 10,000 ft it is about 74 % of sea level, so you need more speed for the same lift.
        V
        Airspeed. It is squared: twice the speed gives four times the lift.
        S
        Wing area, set by root chord, tip chord and span.
        CL
        Lift coefficient: how hard the wing is working. It grows by roughly 0.08 for every degree of angle of attack, the angle between the wing and the oncoming air.

        Worked example. The High-wing trainer weighs about 2,370 lb (10,500 N) and has 162 ft² (15 m²) of wing. At 100 mph at sea level, ½ρV²S is about 18,300 N, so it needs CL ≈ 0.57, which its wing makes at about 4° angle of attack. Fly slower and it must raise its nose to get more CL.

        Every strip, all together. Lift is not the same all along the span: the wingtips leak air round from below, so they carry less, and sweep moves lift outboard. Wingworks works this out with a vortex lattice, the same family of method engineers use in early design. It treats each strip of the wing, tail and fin as a spinning line of air and solves how they all affect one another, so a tapered or swept wing really does stall at its tips first unless you add washout.

        Airfoil. The cross-section matters. Camber (the curve of the centre line) makes lift even at zero angle. Thickness makes the wing stronger and gives it a gentler stall. In a NACA 4-digit name like 2412, 2 is the camber (2 %), 4 is where the camber peaks (40 % of the chord) and 12 is the thickness (12 %).

        Stall: the speed you cannot go below

        CL only keeps rising up to about 13–16° of angle of attack. Past that, the air can no longer follow the curved top of the wing. It breaks away, lift collapses and drag soars. That is a stall, and it has nothing to do with the engine.

        The slowest speed you can fly level is the stall speed:

        Vstall = √( 2 × Weight ÷ (ρ × S × CL max) )

        Lower it with more wing area, a more cambered or thicker airfoil, slats, or less weight. Land at about 1.3 × stall speed. Washout (a negative twist at the tip) makes the root stall first, so the ailerons keep working and a wing does not suddenly drop. In flight, the HUD flashes STALL WARNING and a horn sounds a few degrees before it happens.

        A spin is a stall with rotation. If one wing stalls more deeply than the other, it drops, its angle of attack grows, and it stalls further still: the aircraft falls in a corkscrew. The way out is PARE: power to idle, ailerons neutral, full rudder against the turn, then stick forward to unstall the wing. When the rotation stops, centre the rudder and ease out of the dive. Some aircraft recover by themselves (a Cessna); some need the full drill and a couple of turns (a Mustang). With the flight computer on, it will not let you stall, so turn it off (J) to try one, high up, or take the Spin recovery challenge.

        Drag: what the engine pays for

        Drag comes in two kinds that pull in opposite directions as speed changes.

        • Parasite drag is the air rubbing and pushing on everything: skin friction over the wetted area, the shape of thick or blunt parts, the fuselage's frontal area, the landing gear and the engine cooling. It grows with the square of speed.
        • Induced drag is the price of making lift: the wingtips leave swirling vortices behind. It is biggest when you fly slowly (high CL) and shrinks with a longer, slimmer wing, a higher aspect ratio (span² ÷ area).
        • Wave drag appears near the speed of sound, when shock waves form. Thin, swept wings and a slim fuselage delay it.

        The designer splits drag into these pieces under Forces in level flight, and lists the fuselage's frontal area and drag coefficient.

        Stability: why the CG must lead

        A stable aircraft returns to the attitude it was trimmed for after a bump, without help. In pitch, that comes down to two points along the fuselage:

        • Centre of gravity (CG): where the weight acts. You move it with the mass items on the Airframe tab.
        • Neutral point (NP): where the extra lift from a gust acts. The wing's position and the size and distance of the tailplane set it.

        The gap between them, divided by the wing's mean chord, is the static margin. Aim for 5–20 %. Below 5 % the aircraft is twitchy; above about 30 % it is so nose-heavy you may not have enough elevator to land.

        Static margin = (NP − CG) ÷ MAC

        • Too little margin? Move the mass items forward, move the wing back, make the tailplane bigger, or lengthen the fuselage. The tail volume VH (tail area × tail arm ÷ wing area × MAC) usually sits at 0.4–0.9.
        • Yaw: the fin works like a weathervane and keeps the nose pointed into the wind. You need Cnβ above zero; the fin volume VV is usually 0.03–0.09.
        • Roll: dihedral or a high wing makes the aircraft level its wings after a sideslip, shown by Clβ below zero.

        Why the nose rises when you add power

        An aircraft is trimmed for an angle of attack, not a speed. Add power and it speeds up, the extra speed makes extra lift, and it climbs. It then slows, sinks, speeds up again, in a slow see-saw called the phugoid. Real pilots push the nose down or re-trim. With Flight assist on, the computer holds the flight path instead, so more power simply means more speed.

        Why it wobbles

        A side-to-side, nose-wagging wobble after a roll is the Dutch roll. Strong dihedral with a small fin makes it worse. A bigger fin, a little less dihedral, or the yaw damper in Flight assist calms it.

        Controls and flight assist

        Elevator (W/S) changes the tailplane's lift to tip the nose up or down, which changes the wing's angle of attack. Ailerons (A/D) move opposite ways to roll. Rudder (Q/E) swings the nose left or right. A real aircraft turns by banking: the tilted lift pulls it round. Rudder alone only skids the nose sideways, and once you let go the fin swings it straight back into the airflow. Every surface works harder the faster you go.

        Trim (T) makes the current elevator position the new neutral, so you do not have to hold a key in steady flight.

        Flaps ( [ and ] ) hinge down from the inner part of the wing's trailing edge. They bend the airflow down harder, so the wing makes more lift at the same speed and the aircraft can fly and land slower. They also add drag, which lets it come down steeply without speeding up. Each aircraft has its own notches (a Cessna's 10°, 20°, 30°; a 747's seven), and each has a speed limit: fly too fast and the flaps blow back to a notch the airflow allows. Lowering them pitches the nose: retrim. Deltas such as Concorde have none: their wing makes its landing lift from vortices at a high angle of attack instead.

        Altitude hold (O) and heading hold (U) hand the flying to the flight computer: it keeps the height or the heading you engaged it at. Move the stick and it follows you; let go and it holds the new one.

        Flight assist (on by default) puts a computer between the keys and the surfaces, like a modern airliner or fighter.

        • W/S pitch the nose down or up. Let go and it holds the flight path you were on, the right way up or inverted, re-trimming as the speed changes. Hold it and you can fly a full loop.
        • A/D roll, with no bank limit: hold the key and the aircraft keeps rolling, all the way round, as fast as its ailerons allow. Let go and it stays at that bank. Turn on Auto-level (H) and it rolls the wings level instead.
        • Q/E use the rudder and a matching bank together, for a smooth, coordinated turn. That bank is kept when you let go, too.
        • On the ground W/S rotate the nose at a gentle rate that stops short of a tail strike, and A/D steer the nose wheel. After touchdown the spoilers deploy when you close the throttle.
        • B brakes the wheels on the ground and opens the airbrakes in flight: use it to slow down for a tight turn in a race.

        Its only protections are the ones real fly-by-wire aircraft have: it will not let you stall or over-stress the airframe. Press Assist in the flight bar (or J) to switch it off and move the control surfaces directly, with T to trim.

        Engines and performance

        Climbing needs more power than level flight does. Rate of climb is the spare power (power available minus power needed) divided by weight. The designer's Power chart shows both curves: where they cross is the top speed, and the widest gap is the best climb speed.

        • Propellers are most efficient at moderate speeds. Fixed-pitch propellers are tuned for cruise; constant-speed propellers stay efficient from takeoff to cruise. They lose thrust near Mach 0.6 as the blade tips approach the speed of sound.
        • Jets give nearly constant thrust with speed. An afterburner (X) adds a lot more for supersonic flight.
        • Altitude thins the air: less drag, but also less engine power and less lift, so you fly faster for the same weight.
        • A thrust-to-weight ratio above 1 means it can climb straight up.
        • Engines have weight. A bigger engine is a heavier engine. Piston engines with their propeller weigh about 1.2 kg for every kilowatt; the best jet engines give 5–8 times their own weight in thrust. The designer adds the engine's weight for you, in the nose for propellers and in the tail for jets, so more power also moves the CG.

        What sets the top speed

        In level flight the top speed is where drag grows to equal the most thrust the engine can give. Past that, three hard limits stop real aircraft, and the simulator models each of them:

        • Engine inlet temperature. Air rammed into the intake heats up: at Mach 2 near the ground it reaches about 245 °C. Jet engines must cut thrust once the air reaching them passes about 125 °C, and stop producing thrust near 250 °C. That caps ordinary jets at about Mach 1.5–1.8 near the ground and Mach 2–2.4 high up, however much thrust they have. The HUD shows ENGINE TEMP LIMIT when it happens.
        • Never-exceed speed (VNE). Air loads grow with the square of speed, and past a certain speed the wings and tail start to flutter. Every aircraft has a placarded VNE: 163 kt for a Cessna 172, 800 kt for an F-16. Above it the HUD flashes OVERSPEED with a clacking warning, and a little faster the airframe breaks up.
        • Skin heating. Friction with the air heats the skin. Aluminium loses strength above about 130 °C, which is why Concorde was limited to Mach 2.04. Carbon and glass-fibre composites soften even sooner. The HUD warns SKIN HOT before the structure fails.

        Speeds are shown as indicated airspeed, the speed an airspeed indicator reads from air pressure. It matches true speed at sea level, but reads lower high up where the air is thin. VNE and stall speed are indicated speeds, so they stay the same at any height.

        How it works: the physics engine

        Nothing in Wingworks is canned. Every number on the design page and every moment of flight comes from one physics engine, about 1,400 lines of JavaScript, running in your browser. These are its parts.

        1. A vortex lattice for the lifting surfaces

        The wing, tailplane and fin are cut into strips: 14 across each wing panel, closer together toward the tips where the lift changes fastest, and 7 on each tail surface. Each strip carries a horseshoe vortex: a spinning line of air bound along its quarter chord, with two trailing legs that stream back to infinity. That spinning air is what lift is.

        The rule that fixes the strengths is simple: at each strip's control point, three-quarters of the way back, the air must flow along the surface, not through it. Every vortex induces a flow at every control point (the Biot–Savart law), so this gives one linear equation per strip. Wingworks solves the whole system once when the geometry changes, then reuses the solution in every physics step, so the lattice costs nothing in flight.

        From the lattice come the lift slope, the spread of lift across the span, the downwash the wing throws onto the tailplane, the sidewash on the fin, and the induced drag, worked out far behind the aircraft in the Trefftz plane. Each strip then gets its own section data from its NACA airfoil: thin-airfoil theory for the zero-lift angle and pitching moment, an empirical stall, skin friction from its Reynolds number, and corrections for compressibility below and above Mach 1. Checked against theory, an elliptical wing of aspect ratio 8 comes out at a span efficiency of 0.998, against an ideal of 1.

        2. Trimming for level flight

        Before every flight, and for every point on the design page's charts, the engine has to find how the aircraft balances. Level flight is two equations in two unknowns: lift equals weight, and the pitching moment about the CG is zero. The unknowns are the angle of attack α and the elevator angle δe.

        The solver is a two-dimensional Newton iteration: it guesses α and δe, measures the leftover lift and moment with the full lattice, estimates how each changes with a small nudge of each unknown, and corrects both together. It usually converges in four or five steps. The slope of those moment lines is the static margin, and the same iteration run at full elevator gives the trimmed stall speed.

        3. Engines

        • Propellers turn shaft power into thrust with an efficiency that rises to a peak at the design speed. At low speed the thrust is capped by actuator-disc momentum theory, and it fades as the blade tips approach Mach 1. Power falls with air density, except on supercharged engines like the Merlin, which hold full power up to their critical altitude.
        • Jets lose thrust with density, gain some from ram pressure, and pay for supersonic flight with inlet pressure losses. A hard limit follows the temperature of the air reaching the compressor, which is why an F-16 stops at about Mach 2 and the SR-71's J58s had to turn into ramjets.

        4. Six degrees of freedom, 240 times a second

        The aircraft is a rigid body with a full inertia tensor, built from where the wings, tails, engine and fuselage mass actually sit. Every step the engine works out the airflow over every strip (including what roll, pitch and yaw rates add), the engine thrust, and the force on each wheel from its oleo strut and tyre friction. Then it integrates the motion: Newton's second law for the velocity and Euler's equations for the rotation, with the attitude kept as a quaternion so the aircraft can loop and roll forever without singularities. Running at a fixed 240 Hz means time ×2 flies exactly like real time, only faster.

        The flight computer is a real control law: an outer loop turns your keys into a pitch-rate and roll-rate request, and holds the flight path and bank when you let go. An inner loop closes on the measured rates, scaled by how much control power the surfaces have at the current speed, so a Cessna and an F-22 respond alike. Load-factor and angle-of-attack limits trim the request before it reaches the elevator.

        5. The world

        Every map is one height function of north and east, shared by the physics and the graphics. The physics asks it for the ground under every wheel and every crash point; the graphics sample it into a detailed patch of terrain around you inside a coarser one that reaches the horizon. The airfield is flattened into it, and an approach corridor keeps the 3° glideslope clear on every map.

        The aircraft flies through the air, not over the ground: wind grows with height above the ground (a power law, as over real farmland), gusts swell and ease over a few seconds, and turbulence is filtered random noise whose scale grows with height, as in the Dryden model engineers use. Inside a cloud the air gets rougher and the view whites out. On the carrier, the tyres push against a moving deck, and a tail hook that crosses a wire is pulled to a stop within about 100 m.

        The real aircraft

        The ten real aircraft in the hangar are built from published figures: dimensions, wing area, weight, engine power or thrust, and limits. They are locked, so what you fly is the aircraft, not a guess. For the physics each is reduced to one wing, one tailplane and one fin with the same areas and positions; the 3D model is the real shape.

        • F-22 Raptor. Two F119 engines push it past Mach 1.5 without afterburner (supercruise), and their nozzles swivel to add pitch control when the wings alone are not enough.
        • B-2 Spirit. Four buried F118 engines, no afterburner. Slow to respond and very stable: fly it smoothly.
        • A-10 Thunderbolt II. A thick, straight wing for low, slow flying. Its high-bypass fans give the famous whistle and a modest top speed of about 380 kt.
        • SR-71 Blackbird. The J58 engines work mostly as ramjets above Mach 3, and the titanium airframe tolerates skin temperatures near 300 °C. Climb to 80,000 ft before going for Mach 3.3.
        • F-16 Fighting Falcon. Designed with relaxed stability, so it turns eagerly; reaches Mach 2 high up with afterburner.
        • Concorde. No tailplane, so it lands nose-high at about 160 kt. Use reheat (X) for take-off and to push through Mach 1, then climb above 50,000 ft for Mach 2.
        • Boeing 747-400. Heavy and slow to respond. Fly the approach with the autothrottle (Z) and start the flare early.
        • P-51D Mustang and Spitfire Mk IX. Taildraggers: they sit nose-high and lift off from that attitude. Their supercharged Merlins keep full power up to about 23,000 ft.
        • Cessna 172. The gentlest of all, and the one to learn on.

        Each has its own engine sound, modelled on its real engines.

        Flying it

        Takeoff

        1. Press Take off. Hold R until the throttle reaches 100 % (press X for afterburner on jets).
        2. Keep straight with A/D or Q/E: on the ground both steer the nose wheel.
        3. At the lift-off speed shown in the message, press S gently until the nose is 8–10° up. Too much and the tail scrapes.
        4. Once climbing, press G to raise retractable gear.

        Turning

        Hold A or D until you reach the bank you want, then let go: the bank stays. Add a little S in steep turns to keep the nose up. Roll back the other way to level the wings, or turn on Auto-level to have it done for you.

        Landing

        1. Press Land (or L in flight) to start 5 km out on a 3° approach with the gear down. To set it up yourself, line up with runway 36 from several miles out, lower the gear (G) and slow to about 1.3 × stall speed.
        2. Keep the two pink diamonds centred: the one beside the attitude ball is the glideslope, the one above it is the runway centreline. The four lights left of the runway (the PAPI) show two white and two red when you are on the slope; more red means too low.
        3. Over the runway threshold, ease back a little (the flare) and close the throttle with F.
        4. Touch down under 600 ft/min, then hold B to brake. Press 2 at any time to run time twice as fast.

        Limits. The wings fail at 1.5 × the limit load factor (the certification safety factor). The landing gear collapses above about 10 ft/s of sink. Hitting a hill, a lake or the ground with anything but the wheels ends the flight.

        Recipe: make a design fly-ready

        1. Start close. Open the example nearest your goal in the hangar, then save your own copy as you go.
        2. Size the wing for the weight. Keep wing loading in the typical range and the stall speed low enough to take off from the 9,800 ft (3 km) runway.
        3. Choose the aspect ratio for the job: 7–9 for all-round flying, 15+ for gliding, 3–4 for supersonic speed.
        4. Pick the airfoil: 2412 or 4412 for slow, lifting wings; symmetric 0012–0015 for aerobatics; thin 0004–0006 with slats and sweep for jets.
        5. Place the wing so the static margin is 5–20 %, then fine-tune with the mass position.
        6. Size the tail: tailplane volume 0.4–0.9 and fin volume 0.03–0.09.
        7. Add dihedral (2–5° low wing, 0–2° high wing) until Clβ is negative.
        8. Set incidence so the fuselage is about level in cruise and the trim elevator is small.
        9. Check the engine: climb rate above 500 ft/min, a sensible top speed, and the CG still in place once the engine's weight is added.
        10. Fly it: runway first, then an airborne start to explore.

        Nose swings back after using the rudderWith assist off, rudder only skids the aircraft; the fin points it back into the airflowBank with A/D to turn, or turn Flight assist on so Q/E fly banked turns
        Side-to-side wobble after rollingDutch roll: weak yaw damping, strong dihedralBigger fin, less dihedral, Flight assist on
        Pitch keeps getting worse until it flipsCG behind the neutral pointMass items forward, wing back, bigger tailplane
        Will not lift off before the runway endsToo heavy, too little wing or powerMore wing area, slats, more power, less mass
        Drops a wing at the stall or spinsTips stall before the rootMore washout (negative twist), less taper
        Sinks even at full throttleDrag is more than the thrust availableMore power, longer span, retractable gear
        Breaks up at high speedPast the never-exceed speed: air loads and flutterThrottle back before OVERSPEED, dive less steeply
        Stops accelerating near Mach 2, whatever the thrustThe air reaching the engine is too hotClimb higher, where the air is colder
        Airframe overheatedSkin heating at high MachFly slower, or use the aluminium–titanium structure
        Much heavier after adding thrustBigger engines weigh moreUse only the thrust you need; rebalance the CG
        Wings break in a hard pullPast 1.5 × the limit load factorPull gently, raise the limit load factor, Flight assist on
        Gear collapses on landingSink rate over about 600 ft/minShallower approach, flare before touchdown
        Too nose-heavy to flareStatic margin too largeMass items back or wing forward
        Nose wanders left and rightFin too small (Cnβ near zero)Taller or longer fin, or move it back

        Glossary

        Angle of attack (α)
        Angle between the wing's chord and the oncoming air.
        Aspect ratio
        Span squared divided by wing area. Long, slim wings have a high aspect ratio.
        Camber
        How curved the airfoil's centre line is. More camber, more lift at a given angle.
        Chord
        Distance from the leading edge to the trailing edge. Root chord is at the fuselage, tip chord at the tip.
        Centre of gravity (CG)
        The balance point of all the aircraft's mass.
        Dihedral
        Upward tilt of the wings from root to tip.
        Induced drag
        Drag created by making lift, largest at low speed.
        Indicated airspeed
        The speed an airspeed indicator reads from air pressure. It equals true speed at sea level and reads lower high up.
        Load factor (g)
        Lift divided by weight. 1 g in level flight, more in a pull-up or a turn.
        MAC
        Mean aerodynamic chord: the average chord used as the yardstick for stability.
        Mach number
        Airspeed divided by the speed of sound.
        Never-exceed speed (VNE)
        The highest indicated airspeed the structure is cleared for. Beyond it, air loads and flutter can break the aircraft.
        Glideslope
        The 3° descent path to the runway. The HUD shows it with a pink diamond, and the PAPI lights show it beside the runway.
        Neutral point (NP)
        Where the extra lift from a change in angle of attack acts. The CG must be ahead of it.
        PAPI
        Four lights beside the runway that turn red or white with your approach angle. Two of each means you are on the glideslope.
        Static margin
        Distance from the CG to the NP as a percentage of the MAC.
        Stall
        When the air separates from the wing's top surface and lift collapses.
        Sweep
        How far the wing slants backward from root to tip.
        Taper ratio
        Tip chord divided by root chord.
        Trim
        Setting the controls so the aircraft holds its attitude with no input.
        Washout
        Twist that lowers the tip's angle of attack so the root stalls first.
        Wing loading
        Weight divided by wing area. Higher means faster stall and landing speeds.

        Wingworks
        W / S
        Nose down / up. Let go and the flight path holds.
        A / D
        Roll left / right, all the way round if you hold it. Let go and the bank holds.
        Q / E
        Rudder, with a coordinated bank
        R / F
        Throttle up / down (also ↑ ↓)
        X
        Afterburner on / off
        G
        Gear up / down
        [ / ]
        Flaps up / down a notch
        B
        Wheel brakes on the ground (A / D steer); airbrakes in flight
        2
        Time ×1 / ×2 / ×4
        H · J
        Auto-level · flight computer on / off
        Z
        Autothrottle: hold this airspeed
        O · U
        Altitude hold · heading hold
        I
        Wingman: a real aircraft beside you
        L
        Restart on final approach
        ⌫
        Restart instantly (races and challenges)
        C · M · V
        Camera · sound · paint style
        N · − =
        Map on / off · zoom
        /
        Five Fields: head for the next airfield
        K · Y
        Photo mode · replay the last 40 seconds
        P · Esc
        Pause · back to design
